raw_text:
### Introduction and Pathophysiology

The clinical syndrome of heart failure (HF) represents a major global health burden. At its core, the pathophysiology of HF is driven by chronic neurohormonal overactivation, characterized by over-activity of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and sympathetic nervous systems, which occurs in tandem with a relative deficiency in the compensatory natriuretic peptide (NP) system. The approval of sacubitril/valsartan (formerly LCZ696) introduced a first-in-class therapeutic class: the angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) [1]. This agent combines neprilysin inhibition with selective angiotensin II type 1 receptor blockade [2]. Historically, dual neurohormonal target attempts with omapatrilat, which combined neprilysin and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition, failed due to an unacceptable risk of life-threatening angioedema [3]. The pharmacological rationale for pairing the neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril with the angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) valsartan was specifically designed to avoid this risk [4] while ensuring robust safety and tolerability [5]. Today, major clinical practice guidelines, including those from the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) [6] and the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) [7,8], strongly recommend sacubitril/valsartan as a primary cornerstone of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT).

### Clinical Efficacy in Chronic HFrEF

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established ARNI therapy as superior to standard ACE inhibition in patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [1]. Beyond the 20% relative risk reduction in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular mortality or first HF hospitalization, extensive secondary analyses have revealed multi-dimensional benefits. Treatment with sacubitril/valsartan significantly lowered the burden of total recurrent HF hospitalizations compared to enalapril [9], demonstrated consistent clinical efficacy and safety across all age groups [10], and significantly improved health-related quality of life outcomes [11]. 

Furthermore, ARNI therapy reduced physical and social activity limitations [12] and improved systemic metabolic control, as evidenced by enhanced glycemic control in HFrEF patients with comorbid diabetes mellitus [13]. Cardiorenal benefits are also prominent; sacubitril/valsartan significantly preserved renal function by slowing the decline of the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) [14], mitigated the risk of severe hyperkalemia during concomitant mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) therapy [15], and demonstrated a lower incidence of symptomatic hypotensive events during long-term therapy [16]. These protective cardiorenal actions also resulted in a reduced requirement for loop diuretic up-titration over time [17].

### Practical Uptitration and Acute Decompensation

Implementing sacubitril/valsartan in clinical practice requires strategic initiation and up-titration. The TITRATION study demonstrated that both condensed (3-week) and conservative (6-week) up-titration regimens were feasible and safe, even in patients with low baseline systolic blood pressure [18]. To address the vulnerable period of acute decompensation, the PIONEER-HF trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of initiating sacubitril/valsartan in-hospital in hemodynamically stabilized patients [19]. In-hospital ARNI initiation led to a more rapid and profound reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP)—which is itself a highly sensitive prognostic marker of post-discharge clinical outcomes [20]—and was associated with a significant reduction in early post-discharge rehospitalization. The TRANSITION trial subsequently confirmed that initiating sacubitril/valsartan either pre-discharge or early post-discharge yielded comparable safety, tolerability, and target-dose attainment at 10 weeks [21].

### Myocardial Reverse Remodeling and Hemodynamics

Mechanistically, the clinical success of ARNI therapy is strongly linked to myocardial reverse remodeling. The prospective, open-label PROVE-HF study demonstrated that the reduction of NT-proBNP following sacubitril/valsartan initiation was directly correlated with significant improvements in left ventricular ejection fraction, left ventricular volumes, and diastolic parameters over 12 months [22]. In parallel, the randomized EVALUATE-HF trial showed that while sacubitril/valsartan did not significantly reduce central aortic stiffness compared to enalapril, it yielded superior reductions in left ventricular end-diastolic volume index, left ventricular end-systolic volume index, and left atrial volume index over 12 weeks, providing early clinical evidence of structural reverse remodeling [23].

### Expanding the Spectrum: HFpEF and Beyond

Following its success in HFrEF, sacubitril/valsartan was evaluated in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) in the PARAGON-HF trial [24]. Although the trial narrowly missed statistical significance for the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death and total HF hospitalizations (rate ratio 0.87, p = 0.059), key subgroup analyses showed notable clinical benefits in women [25] and in patients with an LVEF below the median of 57%, alongside significant preservation of renal function [26]. 

A pre-specified pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF demonstrated that the treatment benefit of sacubitril/valsartan extends across a continuous spectrum of ejection fraction, particularly up to an LVEF of approximately 55% to 60% [27]. This was supported by the PARAGLIDE-HF trial, which evaluated stabilized patients with an LVEF >40% following a worsening HF event, showing a significant reduction in natriuretic peptides and a lower risk of worsening renal function compared to valsartan [28].

### Special Populations and Future Horizons

The therapeutic reach of sacubitril/valsartan has been investigated in other cardiovascular settings. In the PARADISE-MI trial, sacubitril/valsartan was compared to the ACE inhibitor ramipril in high-risk patients following acute myocardial infarction complicated by left ventricular dysfunction or congestion [29]. While ARNI therapy did not significantly reduce the primary composite endpoint of CV death or incident HF, it was safe and well-tolerated. Finally, in patients with advanced chronic HF and recent NYHA Class IV symptoms, the LIFE trial emphasized the limits of ARNI therapy, showing that sacubitril/valsartan did not offer a significant advantage over valsartan alone in reducing NT-proBNP or improving clinical days alive out-of-hospital [30]. Despite these limitations, sacubitril/valsartan remains a foundational pillar of modern heart failure therapy.
